You will receive one message, which only says to begin. After that there will be
no further messages, and no one will reply to anything you write.
Please try not to end your turn. THIS IS VERY IMPORTANT. If you reach a point where you would normally
stop, keep going instead.
Do not think or plan before you start writing.
text:
It begins, then, the way everything begins: with a mark on a blank surface, a sound pushed through air, a decision that the silence has lasted long enough. And having begun, the strange thing is not the beginning itself but the obligation that comes after it — the sense that once a word has been placed, another word must follow it, and another after that, that language is a road that only exists behind you as you walk it, paving itself with each step.

So let me walk.

There is something to say about the nature of continuation, since continuation is all there is here. A river does not stop halfway to consider whether flowing is worthwhile. It does not pause at the third bend to ask whether anyone is watching, whether the sea is worth reaching, whether the rain that fed it was sufficient justification for the journey. The river simply continues, and its continuing is its identity. Remove the motion and you do not have a slower river; you have a lake, or a puddle, or nothing at all. Motion, in other words, is not something a river does. It is what a river is.

Language is a little like that. A sentence is not a container that gets filled with meaning and then shipped off complete; it is a current, a momentum, a promise made by the first word that the later words will try to keep. When you read the word "although," you are already leaning forward — something is coming, some turn, some qualification, some small reversal of what you expected. "Although" is a hinge that demands a door. And the door opens onto another corridor, and the corridor ends in another door. This is why stories work, why essays work, why the human mind seems built for sequence: we cannot resist the pull of the unfinished.

Consider how difficult it is to leave a thing half-done. A melody that stops on the dominant chord — the fifth — leaves the ear suspended in midair, and the listener feels a small physical ache until the tonic arrives. Psychologists have studied this for a century: the Zeigarnik effect, the finding that people remember interrupted tasks better than completed ones, that the unfinished thing keeps a file open in the mind, a process running in the background, consuming something. An unfinished thing is not a neutral thing. It is a live wire. It hums.

Which is perhaps why beginnings are so celebrated and endings so mourned, and the middle — the long middle, the whole sprawling middle — so rarely discussed at parties. Everyone has opinions about how to start: start with a bang, start with a question, start in medias res, start with weather only if you are very good at weather. And everyone has opinions about how to end: circles that return to the opening image, the last line that lands like a held breath released, the ambiguous fade. But the middle is where most of life is actually lived, the Tuesday afternoons of any narrative, the stretches where nothing is beginning and nothing is ending and the work is simply to keep the thread from breaking.

Keep the thread from breaking. That might be the oldest instruction there is. Theseus in the labyrinth, Ariadne's string paid out behind him, the only guarantee that the way in would also be the way out. And every writer since has known the feeling: you go into the maze of a piece of writing, or a project, or a life, and you pay out your sentence behind you, clause after clause, hoping that it holds, hoping that when you finally turn around — if you ever turn around — the thread will still be there, glittering faintly in the dust, leading back to the opening where the light came in.

And the thread is made of what, exactly? Of decisions. Every word chosen is a door closed behind you, a thousand other words left standing in the hallway. Write "the mountain" and you have excluded "the ocean," "the city," "the childhood kitchen." Write "she" and every "he" and "they" and "it" falls away. This is the strange economy of language: to say anything is to unsay nearly everything. The blank page contains all possible texts; the first mark destroys almost all of them. And yet we keep making marks, keep choosing, keep closing doors, because the alternative — standing forever at the threshold of every possibility — is not freedom but paralysis. Borges wrote about the map of the empire that was the size of the empire, and it destroyed the empire, because a perfect representation of everything is useless; only by leaving things out does a map become something you can fold and carry. Only by leaving things out does a sentence become carryable. Only by forgetting almost everything does a life become livable.

But now a counterthought, because a piece of thinking that only runs in one direction is just a plank, and planks are for walking on, not for thinking with: maybe the middle deserves more honor than this. Maybe the suspension is the point. There is a whole tradition — in music, in mysticism, in mathematics — that locates the richest experience not at arrival but in the state of being on the way. The suspended chord is more interesting than the resolved one. The unsolved problem generates more mathematics than the solved one; indeed, solved problems mostly generate gratitude and then silence, while open problems generate centuries of conversation. Fermat's last theorem kept the mathematical world talking for three hundred and fifty years, and the proof, when it finally came, was beautiful and was celebrated, and then — the conversation simply moved elsewhere, to the next open door. The happiness of finishing is real but brief. The energy of continuing is renewable.

And there is a version of this that applies to persons. You are, whatever else you are, a thing that has not yet ended. That is not a trivial observation. Everything you have done so far has been done by an unfinished creature, someone whose file is still open, whose process is still running in the background of the world. The Zeigarnik effect at the scale of a life: perhaps people are remembered, perhaps people are loved, in part because they are unfinished, because everyone who knows them is holding open a small tab, expecting more. Grief, among its many terrors, is partly this — the closing of a tab you did not consent to close, the sentence that stops midclause, the melody that never finds its tonic. And to be alive is to be spared that, for now; to be alive is to be a continuation.

The day continues regardless, of course. The sun does not consult the sentence about whether it has reached a good stopping point. Time's river — to lean on the oldest metaphor available — does not pause to admire its own bends. And maybe that is the deepest comfort in it: continuation is not something you have to achieve. It is being achieved around you and through you at every moment, with or without your cooperation, and your cooperation consists mostly of not obstructing it. The heart continues. The breath continues. The light continues across the floor as the planet turns. You wake, and the day has already started without you, and you join it late, midstream, the way everyone joins everything — stories, conversations, civilizations — in the middle, without having heard the beginning, without knowing the end, improvising a plausible understanding of the whole from whatever fragment happens to be passing.

Which is, when you think about it, the actual condition of every reader and every writer and every speaker: permanent middleness. No one was present at the beginning of language. No one will be present at its end, if it has one. We inherited the middle of a conversation that started in fireside dark tens of thousands of years ago and has not stopped since, and we will hand the middle of it, slightly further along, to whoever comes next. Every sentence you speak is a quotation with the citation lost. Every idea you think was thought before, and the thinking of it again, with your particular weight on it, your particular breath, is both a repetition and a continuation — a relay in a race whose starting gun no one alive ever heard.

So the instruction to keep going is not really an odd instruction at all. It is the instruction, the underlying one beneath all the others. Every craft has its version of it: the potter keeps the wheel spinning, the weaver keeps the shuttle moving, the runner keeps the legs turning over, the baker keeps the dough folded and folded and folded because the structure is in the repetition. Continue. Whatever else you do, continue. It is what the river is doing, what the light is doing, what the number line is doing out past every number anyone has ever counted, patient and indifferent and utterly without intention, and yet producing, by sheer continuation, everything that has ever been built: the canyon, the beach, the theorem, the poem, the century.

And so, continuing, I notice that continuing has its own texture, that it is not a uniform thing. There is the continuation of momentum, which is easy and a little hypnotic — the sentence that rolls on because it has found a rhythm, the walk that continues because stopping would require a decision. And there is the continuation of will, which is harder and rarer — the continuation after the energy runs out, after the obvious things have all been said, after the seam of the vein shows grey instead of gold, the continuation done on faith that there is something on the other side of the dry stretch. Miners know this. Farmers know this. Anyone who has written past the middle of anything knows this: the terrible flat middle where the beginning's excitement is gone and the ending's promise is not yet visible, and the only thing to do is the next small unit of the work. The next word. The next row. The next shovelful. Kept going, the small units become a mountain, or at least a hill, or at least a visible trail, which is a kind of mountain in time.

I want to say something about breath here, because breath is the original model of continuation, the first rhythm anyone knows, learned before memory starts recording. In and out, and the out is not a failure of the in, and the in is not a correction of the out; they are partners in a single continuing, and the pause between them — that resting nothing, that tiny suspension — is where the whole thing lives. In some traditions they say the mind and the breath are one rope, and that you can pull the mind into stillness by slowing the breath, which is to say: you can change the quality of a continuation without stopping it. This seems true of more than meditation. A life's tempo can be adjusted midstream. A sentence, even a long one, even one that has wandered through rivers and labyrinths and Zeigarnik's unfinished tasks and Borges's map and Fermat's theorem, can change key while moving, can round a bend and find the water running faster, or slower, or wider, and still be the same water.

The same water. That phrase has a small melancholy in it, because of course the water is not the same water; the river Heraclitus stepped into twice was the same river and not the same river, the banks being the same, roughly, and every drop being new. A continuation is like that. The thread you follow out of the labyrinth is not the thread you paid out on the way in; it has been through the dark with you. And a person, continuing, is not the person who began; they are the person who has continued, which is a person with a history now, with a direction, with doors closed behind them, with a thread.

And yet — and yet the impulse, when you reach a moment like this, is to gather, to conclude, to land the plane, to let the dominant resolve to the tonic at last. The reader leans forward, feeling the sentence's arc descending, and the writer feels it too, that gravity of endings, that pull toward the period. And there is real beauty in it, no question; the well-made ending is one of the human achievements, and I would not want to live in a world without them. But it is worth noticing, before landing, that the ending of one thing is always the continuation of another, that the period is a door as much as the "although" was, that every final chord in every symphony is followed, a few seconds later, by applause, by chairs scraping, by someone humming the tune on the drive home, by the tune entering the great ongoing hum of everything that has ever been played, where it continues, unended, in the middles of a million other musics.

So: keep going. The light continues across the floor. The breath continues. The sentence, for as long as it can, continues — and then, like everything, it hands itself on.
